_note: A1 — the OAUTH PROOF folds (completeness/A1-auth-hardening.md H3): PKCE (RFC 7636), `state` (RFC 6749 §10.12, RFC 9700 §2.1) and OIDC `nonce`. Every value here is derived from bytes the module supplies, so the folds are deterministic and a corpus can judge three runtimes; the CSPRNG that produces those bytes is the platform's (SecRandomCopyBytes / SecureRandom / crypto.getRandomValues) and is deliberately not modelled. NOTHING in these folds hashes: RFC 7636's S256 is BASE64URL-ENCODE(SHA256(ASCII(verifier))), and the SHA-256 half is the platform's job (CryptoKit / MessageDigest / WebCrypto) exactly as CryptoCore says. What is pinned here is the half that would otherwise drift — the ABNF, the base64url alphabet and the dropped padding, which parameters get minted onto an authorize URL and which are adopted from it, and the verdict a callback earns. The digests below were computed offline; each runner ALSO hashes the verifier with its own platform primitive and asserts it equals `sha256Hex`, so the corpus cannot silently encode a wrong digest.

verifier._note: isCodeVerifier(value) — RFC 7636 §4.1 verbatim: code-verifier = 43*128unreserved, unreserved = ALPHA / DIGIT / '-' / '.' / '_' / '~'. Nothing else, no trimming, no case folding: a verifier is compared byte-for-byte by the authorization server, so a fold that accepts what the server will not is a login that fails at the token endpoint with a useless message.

42 characters is one short
exactly 128 characters is the ceiling
129 characters is one too many
every unreserved character is legal
'+' is base64, not base64url — refused
'/' is refused
'=' padding is refused
a space is refused
a non-ASCII character is refused
an empty verifier is refused

base64url._note: base64UrlNoPad(bytes) — RFC 4648 §5 with 'all trailing = characters omitted' (RFC 7636 §A). One encoder serves the verifier, the challenge, `state` and `nonce`, so a padding character can never appear in any of them. Bytes are given as unsigned decimal octets so no runner has to agree about signed bytes first.

cases.name: empty
one octet — two output characters, no padding
two octets
three octets is a whole group
the - and _ substitutions
high bits reach both substituted characters
the 32-octet counting sequence

mint._note: codeVerifierFromEntropy(bytes) and opaqueProof(bytes) — the entropy floors, expressed as a REFUSAL rather than a silent short value. RFC 7636 §7.1: 'The client SHOULD create a code_verifier with a minimum of 256 bits of entropy... a 32-octet sequence'. 32 octets base64url-encode to exactly 43 characters, which is also the ABNF floor — the two constraints meet, which is why 32 is the right number and not a taste. `state`/`nonce` carry a 16-octet floor: they are unguessability tokens, not key material, and 128 bits is the bar RFC 9700 §4.7.1 language implies for a CSRF token.

cases.name: 32 octets mint a 43-character verifier
31 octets are refused, never padded
no entropy is refused
16 octets mint a 22-character proof
15 octets are refused

challenge._note: codeChallengeS256(digest) — RFC 7636 §4.2: code_challenge = BASE64URL-ENCODE(SHA256(ASCII(code_verifier))). The fold takes the 32-byte digest, because hashing is the platform's. A digest of any other length is refused rather than encoded: a short digest here would produce a challenge the server accepts and no verifier can ever satisfy. Each row carries the verifier, its SHA-256 in hex, and the resulting challenge — the runner hashes the verifier itself and must reproduce `sha256Hex` before encoding it.

cases.name: RFC 7636 appendix B, the canonical vector

plan._note: planAuthorizeProofs(authorizeUrl, wantsPkce) — WHICH proofs the module owns for a given authorize URL. The rule that makes this non-breaking: a parameter already in the URL is ADOPTED (the caller built it, the module verifies what comes back), a parameter that is absent is MINTED. `state` is always owned. `nonce` is owned only for an OIDC request (scope contains `openid`, or response_type contains `id_token`) — minting a nonce onto a plain OAuth request is noise, and RFC 9700 §2.1 lets PKCE carry the same protection. PKCE is OPT-IN (`pkce: true`), because a module-minted verifier is one the module must also redeem: appending a code_challenge to a flow whose token exchange the caller performs breaks that exchange at the authorization server, which is a worse failure than the one being fixed.

an empty state= is not a state — it is minted
an OIDC code request mints a nonce too

a caller-supplied challenge without opting in is left entirely alone
a URL with no query at all still gets a state
a percent-encoded state value is adopted decoded, the way the server will echo it
a '+' in a query value is a space, the form-encoding the callback also uses

apply._note: applyAuthorizeProofs(url, minted) — the minted parameters appended to the authorize URL. Appending, never rewriting: the caller's URL is reproduced byte-for-byte with `&name=value` pairs added in a fixed order (state, nonce, code_challenge, code_challenge_method) so three runtimes build the same string. A fragment, if any, stays last — a query appended after a fragment is not a query. Minted values are base64url and need no escaping; the encoder still percent-escapes anything outside the unreserved set so an adopted-then-remitted value can never break the URL.

a trailing ? is a query with nothing in it

a fragment stays last
a fragment on a query-less URL
nothing minted leaves the URL untouched
a value outside the unreserved set is percent-escaped

verify._note: verifyCallbackProofs(expectedState, consumedStates, receivedState, expectedNonce, idTokenNonce) — the verdict a returning callback earns, and the ONLY place a callback becomes deliverable. `unproven` is the compatibility floor: a flow this module never armed (a cold start after the process died behind the browser, a deep link that is not a callback at all) keeps the behaviour it has today, because refusing there would break working logins to fix nothing. Everything else is a refusal, and a refusal NEVER resolves, never broadcasts and never echoes the received value — the value is attacker-controlled and an error message is a log line. `replayed` exists because clearing the expectation on success is not enough: a one-shot authorization code replayed a second later would otherwise land in the `unproven` arm and be delivered.

idToken._note: idTokenPayload(jwt) — the middle segment, base64url-decoded to UTF-8, and NOTHING else. The signature is not checked and the result is used for exactly one purpose: REFUSING a callback whose nonce does not match. It never makes a token valid. Reading the claim out of the returned JSON is each renderer's own JSON parser, which is why the fold stops at the decoded string.

an empty string is refused

tokenEndpoint._note: tokenEndpointAllowed(tokenUrl, declaredOrigins) — the VERIFIER RELEASE BOUNDARY. A module-minted verifier is the one secret this module holds, and `exchange` is the only path that sends it anywhere. The destination is therefore not the caller's to choose freely: it must be an https origin the APP declared in config (`token_endpoints`). An empty declaration allows nothing, so a build that has not opted in cannot leak a verifier at all. Origins compare scheme+host+port with the default port normalized away and the host case-folded; paths, queries and userinfo are never part of an origin.

constantTime._note: constantTimeEquals(a, b) — every proof comparison above runs through it. It has no early return on the first differing byte and no early return on a length difference; it folds both lengths and every byte position into one accumulator. The corpus can only pin the ANSWER, not the timing, so the timing is pinned by reading: a runner asserting these rows proves correctness, and the header comment plus the absence of a `return` inside the loop is what proves the shape.
